title: Fan-out: WhenAll, WhenAny, WhenEach and PLINQ
summary: Combine tasks the right way, process results as they complete with .NET 9's Task.WhenEach, and know when PLINQ helps and when it hurts.

steps.title: Three ways to wait for many tasks
body: - **`await Task.WhenAll(tasks)`**: wait for all; results come back in the order of the tasks; failures are collected (the `await`
throws the first, the returned task holds them all).
- **`await Task.WhenAny(tasks)`**: returns the first task to finish (it does not throw; await the returned task to get its result
or exception). Good for a race or a timeout; a loop of `WhenAny` + remove over *n* tasks costs O(n²).
- **`await foreach (var t in Task.WhenEach(tasks))`** (.NET 9): yields each task **as it completes**, in completion order, in O(n).
Show the first results while the slow ones still run, or stop early.
if (done.IsCompletedSuccessfully) Show(done.Result);   // completed: .Result does not block here

pairs: All results, in a fixed order, before going on

steps.prompt: Five price lookups are started together. They finish in the order 4, 2, 1, 5, 3. In what order does `await foreach (var t in Task.WhenEach(tasks))` hand them to you?
options: All at once, after the last one
steps.explain: `WhenEach` yields in completion order, which is its whole point. `WhenAll` gives results in the original order, but only after everything is done.

steps.title: PLINQ and Parallel.For: CPU work only
body: `.AsParallel()` (PLINQ) and `Parallel.For/ForEach` split **CPU-bound** work over cores using pool threads.
It helps when each item is real computation (hashing, parsing, image work) over a **large, in-memory** set, on a machine with spare
- the work is **I/O** (HTTP, database): PLINQ blocks pool threads waiting. Use async and `Parallel.ForEachAsync` instead;
- the set is small or the work per item tiny: partitioning and merging cost more than they save;
- it runs **inside a web request**: it takes pool threads from other requests; a busy server has no spare cores anyway;
- the lambda touches shared state (a `List.Add`, a counter): a race. Return values and let PLINQ combine them.
`AsOrdered()` keeps the input order at a cost. Always measure (BenchmarkDotNet) before and after.

steps.prompt: What does this print? (`AsOrdered` keeps the input order in the results.)
steps.explain: Without `AsOrdered` the order of the list would depend on scheduling. `Sum` is an aggregation PLINQ combines correctly, whatever the order.

steps.title: The first three answers
prompt: A search page asks several suppliers at once and shows the **first three successful answers** as soon as they exist; failures are
Write **`static async Task<List<string>> FirstThreeAsync(IEnumerable<Task<string>> lookups)`** returning the first three
successful results **in the order they completed** (fewer if there are not three). Do not wait for the remaining lookups once you
`Task.WhenEach` (.NET 9) is the natural tool. The tests complete the lookups one by one in a chosen order.
template: var dojoDone = await Task.WhenAny(dojoTask, Task.Delay(2000)) == dojoTask;
Dojo.Check("It returns without waiting for the last lookup", dojoDone, "Lookup 3 never answers: stop once you have three results.");
if (dojoDone) Dojo.Eq("The first three successes, in completion order", new List<string> { "supplier-4", "supplier-1", "supplier-5" }, await dojoTask);
var dojoFew = await FirstThreeAsync(new[] { Task.FromResult("only"), Task.FromException<string>(new TimeoutException()) });
Dojo.Eq("With fewer successes, it returns what there is", new List<string> { "only" }, dojoFew);
hints: `await foreach (var done in Task.WhenEach(lookups))` gives tasks in completion order. Skip the ones that are not `IsCompletedSuccessfully`.
Add `done.Result` to a list and `break` out of the loop when it has three.
steps.explain: Breaking out of `await foreach` stops waiting; the lookups still running keep running unless you cancel them, so in production pass a token you cancel once you have enough.
